claims.claim: Jupiter is the biggest planet in the solar system.
claims.note: Jupiter has the largest diameter (142,984 km) and mass (1898e24 kg) of the eight planets. Hook (A4): true as stated at second two.

claims.claim: Two and a half times the mass of every other planet combined.
JUPITER / 2.5× the other planets / combined, by mass
Row of the other seven planets at Jupiter's scale: Saturn 0.833, Uranus 0.363, Neptune 0.352, Earth 0.091, Venus 0.087, Mars 0.0485, Mercury 0.035 of Jupiter's radius
But hold Jupiter up next to the Sun, and it looks tiny. (Jupiter drawn at radius 52 beside the Sun at 520)
claims.where: spoken + on-screen: Jupiter beside the Sun
claims.note: Volumetric mean radius 695,700 km vs 69,911 km, ratio 9.95; drawn ratio 10.0 (0.5% off). 'Tiny' is fair at a tenth of the width.

claims.claim: It would take nearly a thousand Jupiters to fill the Sun.
claims.note: Volume ratio 986.5: 'nearly a thousand' is right. Solid spheres would pack fewer; the on-screen 'by volume' carries that reading.

claims.claim: ≈ 1,000 JUPITERS / to fill it, by volume / dots not to scale (1,000 dots spread across the Sun's disc)
claims.note: 986.5 ≈ 1,000. The dot count is labelled approximate and the dot size is labelled not to scale (A6). A Jupiter-sized disc would fit only ~99 times (radius ratio 9.95 squared), so the label is needed and present.

claims.claim: Our Sun is not an average star. It is an unusually big one.
claims.source_checked: arXiv:2104.14972 (LaTeX source, Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' and Sect. 4 text), = Reylé et al., A&A 650, A201 (2021), doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref metadata checked). CDS catalogue J/A+A/650/A201 (Table A.1) refused by the network proxy
claims.note: Rests entirely on claim 9; fix with claim 9. Table 3 counts check, but the step that makes them a size ranking is not sourced (see claim 9).

claims.claim: It is bigger and brighter than over ninety percent of the stars in our part of the galaxy,
claims.source_checked: arXiv:2104.14972 (LaTeX source, Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' and Sect. 4 text), = Reylé et al., A&A 650, A201 (2021), doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref metadata checked). CDS catalogue J/A+A/650/A201 (Table A.1) refused by the network proxy; Kervella et al. arXiv:1611.03495 (alpha Cen A 1.2234 R_sun, B 0.8632 R_sun) as a spot check
claims.note: Table 3 confirmed exactly (A 4, F 8, G 18, K 38, M 249, D 20, N/A 41; Sun excluded), and the paper says the 41 untyped are 36 possible M, 4 possible L, 1 possible WD. The arithmetic holds: 307/337 = 91.1% counting all A/F/G against the Sun, 306/337 = 90.8% with delta Eri. But the margin is under one percent (three more counter-examples drop it below 90%), and two premises have no A2 citation in SOURCES: (a) that every K and M star and white dwarf in the sample is both smaller and dimmer than the Sun. Table 3 gives spectral class, not size or luminosity class, and the paper text never states sizes. (b) 'Reylé also lists four subgiants... delta Eridani (K0 IV) is larger and brighter than the Sun.' The paper text (arXiv source) does not mention subgiants. This would be in catalogue Table A.1 (CDS), which could not be reached, and delta Eri's radius and luminosity have no citation at all. Change needed: in SOURCES 4, cite a standard reference for main-sequence radius and luminosity by spectral type (e.g. Pecaut & Mamajek 2013, ApJS 208, 9, with its table), cite the Reylé catalogue rows (CDS J/A+A/650/A201) that name the subgiants and show no other evolved K star, and cite a paper for delta Eri's radius and luminosity. Otherwise soften to 'bigger than most stars near us'. The claim is very likely true, but it cannot be confirmed as sourced.

claims.claim: THE SUN / bigger than 9 stars in 10
claims.source_checked: arXiv:2104.14972 (LaTeX source, Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' and Sect. 4 text), = Reylé et al., A&A 650, A201 (2021), doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref metadata checked). CDS catalogue J/A+A/650/A201 (Table A.1) refused by the network proxy
claims.note: Same dependency and same fix as claim 9. 9 in 10 is exactly the threshold that the 90.8% worst case only just clears.

claims.claim: because most stars are red dwarfs: small, dim, and everywhere.
claims.source_checked: arXiv:2104.14972 (LaTeX source, Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' and Sect. 4 text), = Reylé et al., A&A 650, A201 (2021), doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref metadata checked). CDS catalogue J/A+A/650/A201 (Table A.1) refused by the network proxy; Anglada-Escudé et al. arXiv:1609.03449
claims.note: M 249 of 337 typed stars = 74% (285/337 = 85% with the 36 possible M among the untyped); the paper's own figure is 58.9 ± 5.8% of 423 typed objects including brown dwarfs (61.3% with estimated types). Every reading is a majority. Scoped by the preceding 'in our part of the galaxy'. 'Small, dim' is what M dwarf means (Reylé's 'low-mass stars' category). Anglada-Escudé gives Proxima ~0.1% solar luminosity and 0.14 R_sun as the example.

claims.claim: 10×10 grid: 8 large bright yellow (G or hotter), 10 orange (K), 5 tiny white (white dwarfs), 77 red (M or untyped)
claims.source_checked: arXiv:2104.14972 (LaTeX source, Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' and Sect. 4 text), = Reylé et al., A&A 650, A201 (2021), doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref metadata checked). CDS catalogue J/A+A/650/A201 (Table A.1) refused by the network proxy
claims.note: The counts are right: 31/379 = 8.2%, 38/379 = 10.0%, 20/379 = 5.3%, 290/379 = 76.5%, total 100. The red group includes 4 possible L (brown) dwarfs among the untyped, which rounding absorbs. But the dots are drawn at different sizes (large, tiny), and SOURCES 9 says 'the dots show class, not size' while nothing on screen says so. A viewer reads the dot sizes as star sizes (A6). Change needed: put a 'not to scale' / 'dots show type, not size' note on screen, or give all dots one size. The 'large' encoding also inherits claim 9's unsourced size premise.

claims.claim: So look at the nearest star to our own. Proxima Centauri, just over four light years away.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive TAP pscomppars (hostname Proxima Cen): sy_dist 1.30119 +0.00034/-0.00035 pc; Anglada-Escudé et al. arXiv:1609.03449 = Nature 536, 437 (2016), doi:10.1038/nature19106 (Crossref checked)
claims.note: 1.30119 pc = 4.244 ly, which is 'just over four'. Anglada-Escudé: 'At a distance of 1.295 parsecs... Proxima Centauri... is the Sun's closest stellar neighbour'.

claims.claim: The closest star to the Sun,
claims.note: 'the Sun's closest stellar neighbour', verbatim support.

claims.claim: and you have almost certainly never seen it. It is almost always too faint for your eyes.
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars sy_vmag 11.01 ± 0.10; Howard et al. arXiv:1804.02001 = ApJL 860, L30 (2018), doi:10.3847/2041-8213/aacaf3 (Crossref checked)
claims.note: V = 11.01. Howard: 'no M-dwarfs are usually visible to the naked-eye'. The March 2016 superflare brightened it ~68× at human-eye cadence, to g' = 6.8, 'at the limit of visibility to trained observers at very dark sites'. That one event is what justifies the 'almost' hedges.

claims.claim: PROXIMA CENTAURI / ≈ 0.15× the Sun's radius (drawn at 14.4 against the Sun's 96)
claims.source_checked: Kervella et al. arXiv:1611.03495 = A&A 598, L7 (2017), doi:10.1051/0004-6361/201629930 (Crossref checked); NASA Exoplanet Archive ps/pscomppars st_rad (default ref Suárez Mascareño et al. 2025, 2025A&A...700A..11M per the archive's own link); Anglada-Escudé et al. arXiv:1609.03449
claims.note: The figures cited are right: Kervella adopts 0.1542 ± 0.0045 R_sun (Table, from the Mann et al. radius-M_K relation), and the archive gives 0.141 ± 0.021. But SOURCES 10 records the disagreement incompletely (A3). Kervella's own text gives the interferometrically measured radius, 0.141 ± 0.007 R_sun (Demory et al. 2009), which excludes 0.15, and Anglada-Escudé also states 'a measured radius of 0.14 R_sun'. Two of the three readings round to 0.14, not 0.15. Change needed: label '≈ 0.14–0.15×' (or '≈ 1/7', 0.143, which is within 8% of every value) and draw at ~13.7 against 96. Otherwise SOURCES 10 must record the 0.141 ± 0.007 measurement and say why the Mann relation value is preferred.

claims.claim: That is what most of the stars around us look like. (the 8 bright G-or-hotter dots fade out)
claims.source_checked: NASA Exoplanet Archive pscomppars st_spectype 'M5.5 V'; arXiv:2104.14972 (LaTeX source, Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' and Sect. 4 text), = Reylé et al., A&A 650, A201 (2021), doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref metadata checked). CDS catalogue J/A+A/650/A201 (Table A.1) refused by the network proxy; Howard et al. arXiv:1804.02001
claims.note: Proxima is M5.5 V, and M dwarfs are 74% of typed stars within 10 pc (claim 11). Implied reading after the previous line, that most are too faint to see: Howard, 'no M-dwarfs are usually visible to the naked-eye'. Note: the 92 dots left after the fade include 10 orange K dots, and some K stars (e.g. eps Eri) are naked-eye stars. The spoken 'most' still holds on the 77 red dots alone.

claims.claim: The star we call ordinary is one of the rare big ones. (Sun shrinks into the grid as one of the 8; THE SUN / one of the few)
claims.source_checked: arXiv:2104.14972 (LaTeX source, Table 3 'Summary of the 10 pc sample' and Sect. 4 text), = Reylé et al., A&A 650, A201 (2021), doi:10.1051/0004-6361/202140985 (Crossref metadata checked). CDS catalogue J/A+A/650/A201 (Table A.1) refused by the network proxy
claims.note: G-or-hotter (A 4 + F 8 + G 18 + the Sun) = 31 of 379 = 8.2%, so 'rare', 'one of the few' and 1 of 8 per 100 hold from Table 3 alone. Even adding delta Eri (32/379) it stays ~8%. 'Big' is relative to the M/K/WD majority. When claim 9's size citation is added, reference it here too.
